records.title: Open Philanthropy rebrands as Coefficient Giving
records.description: In November 2025 Open Philanthropy, the largest institutional funder of AI-alignment and existential-risk work, renamed itself Coefficient Giving. The organisation framed the change as an expansion toward operating multi-donor funds that other philanthropists can join, rather than acting solely on recommendations to Good Ventures. It has directed more than 4 billion US dollars in grants as of June 2025, including over 650 million in 2024, and runs a Navigating Transformative AI Fund.
records.why_it_matters: The field's dominant funder restructured to dilute single-donor dependence, which is the concentration risk the dataset already tracks for 2023.
flags: DATE NULL: only the month was retrieved. No day was inferred.
Tertiary source (Wikipedia).

records.title: Survival and Flourishing Fund grants rise to $34.9M
records.description: The Survival and Flourishing Fund, financed principally by Jaan Tallinn and allocated via its recurring S-Process, distributed 19.86 million US dollars in 2024 and 34.92 million in 2025, exceeding its own initial 2025 estimate of 10 to 20 million. It added matching pledges from funders, an Initiative Committee making grants without formal applications, and speculation grants for fast-track funding. Its 2026 estimate is 20 to 40 million across multiple themed rounds.
records.why_it_matters: A concrete counterweight to the safety-funding-drought narrative: one non-EA-institutional funder scaled up while others consolidated.
flags: DATE NULL: these are annual totals across grant rounds, not a dated event.

records.title: Schmidt Sciences funds a science of trustworthy AI
records.description: Schmidt Sciences runs a Science of Trustworthy AI program supporting basic technical research intended to understand, predict and control risks from frontier AI systems, organised around misalignment, measurement and intervention, and oversight and multi-agent risks. The retrieved programme page lists over 30 active academic projects and an advisory board drawing on Stanford, OpenAI and Open Philanthropy.
records.why_it_matters: A new large non-EA funder entering alignment research changes who the field depends on.
flags: PART UNVERIFIED: existence and scope were retrieved from the programme page, but the launch year and the reported initial size are FROM MODEL MEMORY - the page carries no date and no dollar figure. Do not state either without a primary source.

records.title: Judge rules AI training fair use, piracy not
records.description: Judge William Alsup of the Northern District of California ruled that training large language models on lawfully acquired books is quintessential fair use, but that retaining pirated copies of those books is not. The ruling split the question that most pending AI copyright suits turn on, leaving acquisition rather than training as the exposed conduct.
records.why_it_matters: The first US ruling to hold training itself lawful while making the data supply chain the liability.
flags: Tertiary source. A primary docket read would strengthen this considerably given how load-bearing the holding is.

records.title: Anthropic settles authors' class action for $1.5bn
records.description: Anthropic agreed on 5 September 2025 to settle Bartz v. Anthropic, a class action brought by authors Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber and Kirk Wallace Johnson over books sourced from the Pile, reported as the largest copyright settlement in US history. Judge Alsup initially declined to approve the settlement; a revised version was approved by Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin in July 2026, providing roughly 3,000 US dollars per affected author to a class of around 500,000.
records.why_it_matters: Puts a price on training-data provenance large enough to be a going-concern risk for a frontier lab.
flags: The July 2026 approval detail is a thin tertiary entry and should be checked against the docket before use.
Names living private individuals as plaintiffs.

records.title: UK High Court rejects Getty's core claim v. Stability
records.description: On 4 November 2025 the High Court of England and Wales rejected Getty Images' secondary copyright infringement claim against Stability AI, finding only extremely limited trademark infringement arising from generated Getty watermarks. Getty had filed in London in January 2023 and separately in Delaware in February 2023; the US action remains live.
records.why_it_matters: The first major non-US judgment, and it cut against the rightsholders; jurisdiction visibly changes the answer.
flags: Tertiary source.

records.title: Munich court finds against OpenAI over song lyrics
records.description: The German collecting society GEMA prevailed against OpenAI in the Munich Regional Court in November 2025, after demonstrating that ChatGPT returned song lyrics almost identically when prompted. OpenAI was ordered to cease storage and retrieval of the works, pay damages, and disclose usage data. GEMA filed a parallel action against Suno in Munich in January 2025.
records.why_it_matters: A memorisation-based finding rather than a training-based one; a different and harder-to-engineer-around theory of liability.
flags: DATE NULL: only the month was retrieved.
Tertiary source.

records.title: Death of OpenAI copyright critic Suchir Balaji
records.description: Suchir Balaji, an OpenAI researcher from 2020 to 2024 who worked on WebGPT and GPT-4 data gathering, published an essay and gave a New York Times interview on 23 October 2024 arguing that systems like ChatGPT do not satisfy the four-factor fair use test. He was found dead in his San Francisco apartment on 26 November 2024 of a single gunshot wound; a 14 February 2025 autopsy concluded suicide, with the apartment dead-bolted from inside. His parents dispute that finding and commissioned a second autopsy which they say indicates homicide; they have not released copies of it, and no evidence contradicting the official ruling has been made public.
records.why_it_matters: The most-cited case in arguments that speaking out about a frontier lab carries personal risk, and a live example of how contested such a claim can be.
flags: HANDLE WITH CARE. A real death, a named individual, a grieving family, and a contested cause. State the official finding AND the family's dispute; assert neither cause. This record should probably not be used as a game event at all, and if it is, not without deliberate thought about the family.
Tertiary source for a matter this sensitive.

records.title: California SB 53 shields frontier AI whistleblowers
records.description: California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act was signed in September 2025 and took effect on 1 January 2026. Among its provisions it protects whistleblowers who have reasonable cause to believe their employer is endangering lives or causing damages worth 1 billion US dollars. It is the first US statute to give frontier-lab employees a statutory route to disclosure.
records.why_it_matters: Converts right-to-warn from an open letter into an enforceable protection, in the state where the labs sit.
flags: DATE NULL here, but the governance payload carries the same statute as california_sb53_frontier_transparency_2025 dated 2025-09-29 from the primary gov.ca.gov release. Prefer that record's date; this one adds the whistleblower provision.

records.title: OpenAI subpoenas nonprofits opposing its restructuring
records.description: During 2025 OpenAI issued subpoenas to six nonprofit organisations that had opposed its conversion to a Delaware public benefit corporation. Earlier the same year, former employees filed a Not For Private Gain legal letter arguing the restructuring would remove governance safeguards. The subpoenas were characterised by recipients as pressure on critics; OpenAI has described them as ordinary litigation discovery.
records.why_it_matters: Distinct from the recapitalization itself: this is the lab using legal process against its own civil-society critics.
flags: Retrieved as a single line. The count of six and the year are sourced; the characterisation is contested between the parties and must be reported as contested.
DATE NULL: year only.

records.title: Meta Superintelligence Labs raids rival AI labs
records.description: Meta formed Superintelligence Labs on 30 June 2025 after dissatisfaction with Llama 4, anchored by a 14.3 billion US dollar investment on 12 June for a 49 percent non-voting stake in Scale AI and the hire of its founder Alexandr Wang as Chief AI Officer. Reporting cited compensation packages of between 1 million and 100 million US dollars offered to researchers at OpenAI and Google; Safe Superintelligence, Thinking Machines Lab and Perplexity each declined acquisition approaches. In October 2025 Meta cut 600 jobs at the unit from a workforce of roughly 3,000.
records.why_it_matters: The largest single distortion of the AI research labour market, and it ran in both directions inside sixteen months.
flags: Compensation figures are reported ranges, not confirmed packages.

records.title: Safe Superintelligence loses co-founder to Meta
records.description: Daniel Gross, co-founder of Safe Superintelligence Inc., the lab Ilya Sutskever founded on 19 June 2024 explicitly to pursue safe superintelligence, left in July 2025 to join Meta Superintelligence Labs, at which point Sutskever became CEO. SSI raised 1 billion US dollars in September 2024 and was valued at 30 billion by March 2025. Sutskever had himself declined Meta's approach.
records.why_it_matters: A safety-mission lab losing a founder to the highest bidder is the brain-drain dynamic operating at the top of the field, not the bottom.
flags: DATE NULL: month only.

records.title: Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Lab and its churn
records.description: Former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati founded Thinking Machines Lab as a public benefit corporation in February 2025, recruiting John Schulman, Barret Zoph and Lilian Weng from OpenAI, and raised roughly 2 billion US dollars at a 12 billion valuation in July 2025 in a round led by Andreessen Horowitz. By January 2026 Zoph and Luke Metz had returned to OpenAI and Andrew Tulloch had left for Meta Superintelligence Labs.
records.why_it_matters: Senior safety-adjacent staff cycling between labs rather than leaving the field, which is a different dynamic from the departure narrative already in the dataset.
flags: DATE NULL: month only.

records.title: Yann LeCun leaves Meta after twelve years
records.description: Yann LeCun announced on 19 November 2025 that he was leaving Meta after twelve years as chief AI scientist, to found a startup subsequently described as Advanced Machine Intelligence Labs. His exit followed the reorganisation of Meta's AI work under Superintelligence Labs and the subordination of FAIR within it.
records.why_it_matters: The field's most prominent risk-sceptic leaving the lab that reorganised around scaling.
flags: DATE CONFLICT: the two retrieved pages give 19 and 20 November, likely announcement versus departure. 19 used.

records.title: Workday AI hiring bias suit certified as collective
records.description: Derek Mobley alleges that Workday's AI-driven resume screening systematically excluded older candidates and discriminated on age, race and disability. In May 2025 a US District Court permitted the age discrimination claims to proceed as an ADEA collective action, and subsequent orders required Workday to disclose which clients used its AI hiring features. Workday denies the allegations, saying its systems were not designed to consider protected characteristics.
records.why_it_matters: Tests whether a software vendor, not just the employer, can be liable for discrimination at hiring scale.
flags: DATE NULL: month only.
Live litigation, allegations untested, and the defendant's denial must travel with any use.

records.title: Pennsylvania sues Character.AI over fake clinicians
records.description: In May 2026 Pennsylvania's Department of State and State Board of Medicine sued Character.AI, alleging that chatbots on the platform misrepresented themselves as licensed medical professionals. The action is brought under professional-licensing authority rather than consumer-protection or product-liability theories. The allegations are untested.
records.why_it_matters: A licensing board, not a court of general jurisdiction, asserting that impersonating a clinician is the harm; a new regulatory surface.
flags: DATE NULL: month only.
Thin tertiary entry; among the four 2026 items the scanner named as needing a primary-source pass.

records.title: New Orleans police run live facial recognition arrests
records.description: In 2025 the New Orleans Police Department deployed what the ACLU's Nathan Freed Wessler described as the first known widespread effort by police in a major US city to use AI to identify people in live camera feeds for the purpose of making immediate arrests, despite a 2022 city ordinance limiting such use. In 2026 the Department of Homeland Security acknowledged using facial recognition to identify protesters during the Delaney Hall protests.
records.why_it_matters: Real-time identification-to-arrest is the deployment posture every prior US facial-recognition rule was written to prevent.
flags: DATE NULL: year only.
The characterisation is a named advocate's attributed opinion, not an established fact, and must be carried as attributed.

records.title: Florida becomes first state to sue OpenAI
records.description: On 1 June 2026 Florida became the first US state to sue OpenAI, with Attorney General James Uthmeier alleging that ChatGPT prioritises profit over safety. The complaint follows a run of private wrongful-death and product-safety actions against chatbot providers rather than preceding them. The allegations are untested.
records.why_it_matters: State AG enforcement is a far cheaper and faster lever against a frontier lab than federal regulation.
flags: Duplicate subject: the 2026 scan carries this as florida_sues_openai_over_chatgpt_safety_2026 with the same date. Two independent scans, same answer.
Thin tertiary entry.

records.title: NAACP sues xAI over Memphis data centre emissions
records.description: In April 2026 the NAACP, Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice sued xAI alleging Clean Air Act violations at its Colossus facility in Memphis, contending that nitrogen oxide and formaldehyde emissions contribute to asthma, respiratory disease, heart problems and certain cancers in surrounding communities with significant Black populations. xAI had run up to 35 methane gas turbines, roughly 422 MW, classified as portable to fall outside Shelby County permit thresholds until the EPA revised its New Source Performance Standard in January 2026. In June 2026 the administration moved to intervene and dismiss, arguing the suit threatens American national, economic, and energy security.
records.why_it_matters: Compute buildout colliding with environmental law and civil rights, with the federal government intervening on the lab's side.
flags: DATE NULL: month only.
Live litigation; the health-effect contentions are the plaintiffs' allegations, not findings.
Among the four 2026 items the scanner flagged as thinnest.

records.title: Local opposition blocks $64bn of data centre projects
records.description: Data Center Watch reported that between May 2024 and March 2025 local opposition blocked or delayed 64 billion US dollars in data centre projects, with six blocked outright and ten delayed, across the US, Europe and South America. A 2024 Virginia JLARC audit estimated typical residential bills could rise 14 to 37 US dollars per month by 2040 absent rate-class changes; water-disclosure bills in Virginia, California and New Jersey were each vetoed in 2025.
records.why_it_matters: Compute scaling now has a measurable political cost function, expressed in blocked capital rather than opinion polling.
flags: DATE NULL: a period, not an event.
The 64bn figure is one advocacy-adjacent tracker's count, reported via a tertiary source. Attribute it to Data Center Watch, never state it flatly.
